The owner's standing rule applies: where a place has no researched rule, the game draws from a realistic national range, stable per place across saves, and records that the value is drawn rather than known; a real rule overrides. So a usable answer is the national spread plus the state general-law rules that override it, not a list of every city.

Asked again by lamontae on 2026-09-22 at 20:02Z, in the same message where he said every town in America should be tested, not just Kentucky, and that a locality without researched rules should get a realistic blanket rule and be marked as such.
question: For American cities, towns and counties, what are the rules for the local chief executive and governing body that a life simulation needs to let a person run for and hold local office? Specifically: the forms of municipal government in use (mayor-council strong and weak, council-manager, commission, town meeting) and roughly how common each is by place size; whether the mayor is directly elected, chosen by the council from its members, or rotates, and how common each is; the usual term length and whether term limits exist; the qualifications for local office (minimum age, residency period in the municipality or ward, being a registered voter); whether local elections are partisan or nonpartisan and when they are held (odd years, spring, consolidated with state elections); and where a state's general municipal law fixes any of these for all its municipalities rather than leaving them to each charter. Also the county equivalent: an elected county executive or mayor versus a commission or board, and how common each is.

sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Cover how local ballots are counted and citizen petitions, per state, from a research synthesis. Silent on the form of government, mayors, term lengths, term limits and qualifications.
Show four large consolidated governments with no local government on screen, and D.C. named 'City of Washington Dc'. They say nothing about what the right local offices are.

title: Mayors, councils and county executives: who holds local office and how
usableAnswer: A national distribution for each item (form of government by place-size band, mayor selection method, term length, term limits, age and residency qualifications, partisan or nonpartisan, election timing), expressed as ranges or shares the game can draw from, plus the list of states whose general law fixes a value for every municipality, with the instrument named. Large-city specifics are welcome but optional; the distribution and the state overrides are what the game needs, because the game must fill every town with something realistic and mark where the value is drawn rather than known.
whyItMatters: The owner wants a player able to run for office in every town in America, including small ones nobody has heard of. Local office is the first rung of a political career and today the game offers state legislative seats and governors but not a mayoralty or a council seat, and prints that no local government exists for some of the largest cities in the country.

answer.summary: National distributions, not state law. ICMA 2018 survey (published July 2019): 12,761 governments surveyed, 4,109 or 4,115 responses (the report gives both), 32.2% response. Form: council-manager 48.2%, mayor-council 38.2%, commission 3.2%, town meeting 8.1%, representative town meeting 2.3%; mayor-council is the most common form under 5,000 residents. Chief official directly elected 75.6%, chosen by the council 21.3%, by rotation 1.6%; chief terms 4 years 49.4%, 2 years 28.6%; term limits 8.6%. Councils: 5 seats 39.3%; at-large 68.0%; about 64% four-year terms; 80.8% staggered; term limits 8.7%. Party labels on council ballots 30.1% overall, 14.9% for cities. Form set by charter 47.3%, by state law 26.1%. Counties (NACo): about 700 elected executives and about 1,300 appointed administrators, 83 with both; 97% of elected executives serve four-year terms; 8% have term limits; boards elected by district 53%, at-large 29%, mixed 18%.
